summary: Defines a Management Information Base (MIB) module for monitoring the Name Server function of a Fibre Channel network. The Name Server lets Fibre Channel ports register and look up names and attributes. It is a proposed standard for use with network management protocols such as SNMP.

plainLanguage.summary: A phone book for a storage network. This document says how a management tool can read that phone book to see who is listed.

questions: snmp mib for fibre channel names
what is the fibre channel name server mib
what is a name server information subset
how to secure fibre channel mib access
subtitle: SNMP objects that let a management tool look inside the Name Server of a Fibre Channel storage network.

tldr.problem: Fibre Channel networks keep a Name Server where ports register and look up names, addresses and other attributes, but there was no standard way to monitor it over SNMP.
tldr.mechanism: The T11-FC-NAME-SERVER-MIB module defines tables of registered port data, request, RSCN and reject statistics, and a notification sent when a registration request is rejected.
tldr.outcome: Any SNMP manager can read the same Name Server objects from different vendors' switches. It is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted or updated.

today: RFC 4438 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2006, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It depends on the companion RFC 4439 for shared textual conventions.

sections.title: What the Name Server MIB Covers
sections.content:
RFC 4438 defines a Management Information Base (MIB) module for the Name Server function of a Fibre Channel (FC) network. The Name Server lets FC ports register and discover attributes such as names, addresses, types and features, at various protocol layers.

The module is written in SMIv2 and is meant to be read through the Internet-Standard Management Framework, usually with SNMP. It lets a manager monitor the Name Server and configure a few of its parameters. The module defines no managed actions that can be invoked via SNMP.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a school office with a sign-in book listing every student and room. This document lets a helper check that book from far away without walking in.

sections.title: Fibre Channel and the Name Server
sections.content:
Fibre Channel is a high-performance serial channel that carries higher-level protocols such as SCSI command sets and IP. Its end points are N_Ports, connected through a Fabric of switches or by a point-to-point link. Many components have globally unique names, typically formatted as World Wide Names (WWNs). Each port also has a 24-bit address identifier, and in a fabric a switch assigns it dynamically.

The Name Server lets N_Ports and NL_Ports register and discover attributes. Requests and responses travel in Common Transport information units (CT_IUs). Registration may be done by a third party, though the Name Server may refuse it. Because polling the Name Server for changes is costly, the Registered State Change Notification (RSCN) mechanism lets a port ask to be told when relevant information changes. The Name Server itself is defined in FC-GS, and the latest version cited is FC-GS-4.
sections.plainLanguage: Every device in the storage network has a long unique name and a short address. The Name Server is the helper that matches one to the other when asked.

sections.title: How the MIB Is Organized
sections.content:
Every table is indexed by at least fcmInstanceIndex and t11NsInfoSubsetIndex. The first identifies a Fibre Channel management instance, a separable managed piece of FC functionality imported from the FC Management MIB (RFC 4044). One SNMP agent may have several AgentX sub-agents, each implementing a different instance.

The second index identifies a Name Server Information Subset. The information registered with the Name Server is treated as one or more subsets, reachable through different agents or contexts, different management instances, or the same instance. The union of the subsets is the full registered set, and the subsets may overlap or one may hold everything.

Fabric-related information is also indexed by a Fabric Index, because FC-SW-4 allows multiple Virtual Fabrics. In a fabric conformant to FC-SW-3 its value is always 1.
sections.plainLanguage: The phone book can be split into several copies kept in different offices. Each copy gets a number so a tool knows which one it is reading.

sections.title: Registered Data and Statistics
sections.content:
The MIB has six groups. t11NsDBGroup says whether Name Server operation is local to a particular switch and holds the information currently registered in a subset. The registration table, t11NsRegTable, mirrors what ports registered.

Three statistics groups count requests (t11NsRequestStatsGroup), Name Server RSCNs (t11NsRscnStatsGroup) and rejects (t11NsRejectStatsGroup). Each is conditionally mandatory: it is required only for an implementation that counts those particular statistics. The intent is that implementations that do capture them expose them through the same objects. The statistics table also has t11NsRejects, a counter of rejected requests, and t11NsDatabaseFull, which is true when the Name Server cannot allocate space for a new entry.

The agent MUST report the actual registered values even if they are incorrectly formatted. For that reason the two IP address objects are OCTET STRINGs, so that they can hold values an InetAddress could not.
sections.plainLanguage: The tool can read each entry in the phone book and also see counts, like how many questions were asked and how many were turned away. If the book is full, it can see that too.

sections.title: Rejects and Notifications
sections.content:
When the Name Server rejects a request, the reject carries a reason code, an explanation and a vendor code. The MIB stores the actual values present in the reject, even if they were not appropriate. The reason code convention has 12 values, from none(1) through vendorError(12). The explanation convention has 26 values, such as portNameNotRegistered(3), accessDenied(17) and databaseFull(26).

The notification t11NsRejectRegNotify is generated when a request to register information in a subset is rejected, provided t11NsInfoSubsetRejReqNotfyEnable is true for that subset. It reports the switch WWN, the port name, the rejected command string and the three reject codes. The enable object defaults to false.
sections.plainLanguage: When the office says no to a request, it writes down why. The tool can be told to ring a bell each time that happens.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Only one object is read-write or read-create: t11NsInfoSubsetRejReqNotfyEnable, which turns the notifications on or off. SET operations without proper protection can hurt network operations.

Readable objects may also be sensitive. The text names t11NsRegTable, which holds information about registered Nx_Ports, and t11NsStatsTable, which holds statistics and state about the Name Server. Access to GET and NOTIFY should be controlled, and values may need encrypting in transit. Versions of SNMP before SNMPv3 lack adequate security. The RFC RECOMMENDS SNMPv3 with cryptographic security and says deploying older versions is NOT RECOMMENDED.
sections.plainLanguage: The list shows who is connected, so only trusted people should see it. Use a strong lock, which here means SNMPv3.
